chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hisham ibn Salim, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'It is from the right that the rider says to the walker, "The road" (Make way). And in another copy: "It is from the inequity that the rider should be saying to the walker, "The road" (Make way)."'

key_terms.الرَّاكِبُ: The rider (one on a mount or vehicle)
key_terms.الطَّرِيقَ: The road (used here as a command to make way)
key_terms.الْحَقِّ: The right (legitimate entitlement or proper conduct)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic etiquette for riders and pedestrians sharing the road according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi presents a nuanced jurisprudential perspective on social etiquette, where the act of a rider asking a pedestrian to yield is framed as a 'right' (haqq) in one version and 'injustice' (jawr) in another, reflecting the flexibility of Islamic manners based on context. Scholars highlight this duality to illustrate that while hierarchical privileges exist, they must be exercised with humility to avoid arrogance, aligning with the Shia emphasis on adab (etiquette) in daily interactions. The variation in wording underscores the importance of intention and manner in determining whether a social interaction upholds justice or veers into inequity.
